deep.reconstruction:
Context (end of previous page): in his 'Observatio maximi momenti' Euler says he had assumed that x^2 - n y^2 = (p^2 - n q^2)^3 forces x + y√n = (p + q√n)^3, so that x = p^3 + 3npq^2 and y = 3p^2 q + n q^3.

(1) Counterexample. 16^2 - 3·23^2 = 256 - 1587 = -1331 = (-11)^3 = (1 - 3·2^2)^3. By the old rule 16 + 23√3 would equal (1 + 2√3)^3. It does not, because (1 + 2√3)^3 = 37 + 30√3. Only the norms agree: 16^2 - 3·23^2 = 37^2 - 3·30^2 = -1331.

(2) Remedy. If x^2 - n y^2 = (p^2 - n q^2)^3, there exist f, g with x + y√n = (f + g√n)(p + q√n)^3 and f^2 - n g^2 = 1. For x = 16, y = 23, n = 3, p = 1, q = 2, Euler computes f and g by division: f + g√3 = (16 + 23√3)/(37 + 30√3). He reports f = -1478/1331, g = -371/1331, satisfying f^2 - 3g^2 = 1. He concludes that such coefficients cannot be guessed.

(3) Origin of the case. Euler wanted (x + y)(x^2 + y^2) to be a cube, which needs x + y = 4A^3 and x^2 + y^2 = 2B^3. He set x^2 + y^2 = 2(a^2 + b^2)^3 and states x = a(a^2 - 3b^2), y = b(3a^2 - b^2), i.e. Re and Im of (a + ib)^3. He found x = 13, y = -9: x + y = 4 and x^2 + y^2 = 250 = 2·5^3, so the product is 1000 = 10^3. From this he derived x = 7·37·61 = 15799, y = 9·13·229 = 26793. My verification: x + y = 42592 = 4·22^3 and x^2 + y^2 = 2·785^3, so the product is 34540^3.

(4) Problem: find coprime x, y with x^2 - 3y^2 a cube. Without coprimality the case is trivial: x = a(a^2 - 3b^2), y = b(a^2 - 3b^2). In general put x + y√3 = (f + g√3)(p + q√3)^3 and take the conjugate. Then x^2 - 3y^2 = (f^2 - 3g^2)(p^2 - 3q^2)^3, so f^2 - 3g^2 = 1.
- Solutions: (1,0), (2,1), (7,4), (26,15), and in general powers of 2 + √3.
- (p + q√3)^3 = P + 3Q√3 with P = p(p^2 + 9q^2), Q = q(p^2 + q^2).
- Hence x = fP + 9gQ and y = gP + 3fQ, with f, g of either sign.
- For p = 1, q = 2: P = 37, Q = 10, so x = 37f + 90g and y = 37g + 30f.
- (f,g) = (1,0) gives (37,30); (2,1) gives (164,97); (2,-1) gives (16,23), up to sign. This is the 'difficult' case.

(5) Generalisation to x^2 - n y^2. Take f^2 - n g^2 = 1 and (p + q√n)^3 = P + Q√n with P = p(p^2 + 3nq^2), Q = q(3p^2 + nq^2). The next page gives x = fP + ngQ and y = gP + fQ.
errors: Sign slip: (16 + 23√3)/(37 + 30√3) = 1478/1331 - (371/1331)√3, so f = +1478/1331 and g = -371/1331. Euler (or the printed edition) has f = -1478/1331. Since f^2 - 3g^2 = 1 holds for either sign, his check does not catch it.

The rational f, g come from pairing 16 + 23√3 with (1 + 2√3)^3 instead of its conjugate. Pairing the conjugates gives the unit 2 - √3: 16 - 23√3 = (-2 + √3)(1 + 2√3)^3. Equivalently, -16 + 23√3 = (2 - √3)(1 + 2√3)^3. The remark that such coefficients 'cannot be divined' is therefore an artefact of the choice of conjugate, as his own later integral solution (f, g) = (2, -1) shows.
With f = 2, g = -1 the formulas give x = -16, y = 23, not x = 16. This is harmless since x^2 - 3y^2 depends only on x^2.

The 'in genere' formula is miswritten. As printed, the right sides ½(2+√3)^n + ½(2-√3)^n and ½(2+√3)^n - ½(2-√3)^n are f and g√3 respectively, not f + g√3 and f - g√3. Correctly, f + g√3 = (2 + √3)^n and f - g√3 = (2 - √3)^n.

In the (x+y)(x^2+y^2) remark, x = a(a^2 - 3b^2), y = b(3a^2 - b^2) gives x^2 + y^2 = (a^2 + b^2)^3, not 2(a^2 + b^2)^3. The required factor (1+i) is omitted. Indeed 13 - 9i = (1+i)(2-i)^3, while a = 2, b = -1 in his formulas yields (2, -11). This is the very same 'missing factor' phenomenon the page is about.

Unjustified completeness claim: 'all cases' follow by varying f, g. Because ε^3 can be absorbed into the cube, f, g need only range over ±1, ±ε, ±ε^2 with ε = 2 + √3. p, q must also vary over all representations of the cube root of the norm. For general n the statement tacitly needs unique factorisation, which fails for many n; it does hold for Z[√3].

results.what: Recognition that x^2 - n y^2 = (p^2 - n q^2)^3 does not imply x + y√n = (p + q√n)^3, with explicit counterexample 16 + 23√3 vs (1 + 2√3)^3 = 37 + 30√3
results.modern_name: Unit ambiguity in factorisation in real quadratic orders (Z[√3]); failure of the naive cube-root step used in Euler's Algebra
results.usually_credited_to: Gap in Euler's Algebra (1770) usually noted by later authors (Lagrange's additions; Gauss/Kummer era for the general theory)

results.what: Correct parametrisation x + y√n = (f + g√n)(p + q√n)^3 with f^2 - n g^2 = 1 (Pell units), giving x = fP + ngQ, y = gP + fQ
results.modern_name: Elements of given norm = unit × cube (unit group of Z[√n] via the Pell equation)
results.usually_credited_to: Implicit in Lagrange/Gauss; systematic treatment by Dirichlet (unit theorem) and Kummer/Dedekind

results.what: Solutions of f^2 - 3g^2 = 1: (1,0), (2,1), (7,4), (26,15), generated by powers of 2 + √3
results.modern_name: Pell equation, fundamental unit of Z[√3]

results.what: Coprime solutions of (x + y)(x^2 + y^2) = cube: (13, -9) and (15799, 26793)
results.modern_name: Rational points via Gaussian-integer parametrisation / chord-tangent derivation

deep.surprise_reason: The note shows Euler explicitly catching the gap in his own cube-root argument (the one used in the Algebra) and repairing it with Pell units. That is a conceptually interesting anticipation of unit ambiguity in algebraic number theory. However, it is restricted to units (no awareness of non-unique factorisation), it contains slips, and it was printed in the Opera Posthuma in 1862, so historians may know it.

checkable.asserts: Euler's large solution satisfies x + y = 4A^3, x^2 + y^2 = 2B^3.
13 - 9i needs the factor (1+i), absent from Euler's stated parametrisation.

transcription_corrections: Transcription matches the image on the key numbers (f = -1478/1331, g = -371/1331, y = -9, x = 13, x = 7.37.61, y = 9.13.229). The minus sign on f is in the printed source, not an OCR error.
In the last displayed formula, '[=P]' and '[=Q√n]' are editorial brackets in the printed edition. In the printed line, the Q-term reads q(3pp + nqq)√n.
'brevitatis gr.' is the printed abbreviation of 'brevitatis gratia'.
